title: One command, four hours
teaches: Blast radius, cells and shuffle sharding, static stability, safe changes, and dependency loops

blocks.text: At 9:37 a.m. Pacific time on Tuesday 28 February 2017, an engineer on Amazon's S3 team was investigating why S3's billing system was running slowly in US East, Amazon's largest region, in northern Virginia. Following an established playbook, the engineer ran a command to take a small number of servers out of service from one of the subsystems the billing system used. One of the command's inputs was typed wrongly, and the tool removed a much larger set of servers.

Among them were servers for two subsystems that every S3 request in the region needed. The **index** subsystem held the metadata and location of every object in the region, and every read, list or write of an object went through it. The **placement** subsystem chose where new objects would be stored. Engineers had to restart both from scratch, and S3 in US East stopped serving requests. Amazon's post-incident summary noted that neither subsystem had been fully restarted in the larger regions for many years, and that both had grown substantially since then; the restart, with its safety checks, took far longer than anyone expected. Reads recovered at 1:18 p.m. and writes at 1:54 p.m., just over four hours after the command ran.

Much of the web stopped with it, because thousands of companies kept their images, files and pages in S3. So did other Amazon services in the region that stored data in S3. For the first two hours, Amazon could not even mark S3 as down on its own status page, because the page's administration console stored its status icons in S3.

Nothing in S3 had failed on its own. One person made one mistake with a tool that allowed it, and the mistake affected every customer in the region. In this lesson, we will study the designs that limit how far a single mistake or failure can reach, and the designs that keep a system running while a dependency is down. In Lesson 18, we kept one slow dependency from dragging its callers down; here, we examine what happens when an entire subsystem fails.

The **blast radius** of a failure is the share of users, requests or data it affects. Engineers measure this in two ways: how much damage one change can cause, and how much damage one bad input can cause. We can calculate either from the system design by listing the customers whose requests pass through each component; the largest share is the design's worst-case blast radius. A bad input that crashes whichever server handles it, such as a malformed query that triggers a bug, is called a **poison request**. When the client gets no answer and retries, the load balancer sends the retry to another server, which crashes as well.[^poison]

In a single shared fleet, any customer's request can land on any server, so one retried poison request can take down every server in turn. The first defence is **cells**, where engineers split the fleet into several complete, independent copies of the service, each with its own servers and data, and assign each customer to one cell. A thin routing layer in front directs each request to its customer's cell. A component failure, a bad deployment or a poison request then affects only the customers in that single cell.

Cells trade away resource pooling. Each cell needs its own spare capacity to handle its own peak load, so the fleet as a whole runs at lower utilisation than a single shared pool, and engineers must migrate any customer who outgrows a cell. We must also keep the router small and simple, because it is the one component every customer shares. The router uses a lookup table mapping customers to cells rather than a hash function, so we can move one customer without moving others, and assign new customers to the newest cell with spare capacity. The control plane manages this table, while the router continues routing with its last cached copy if the control plane goes down, a property we cover in Part 3.

**Shuffle sharding** achieves better isolation on the same number of machines. Instead of fixed cells, each customer is assigned a random subset of servers. Suppose we have 8 servers and assign 2 servers to each customer. There are 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 unique pairs, so 28 customers can each get a distinct pair. A poison request from one customer crashes their 2 servers. Any other customer shares at most 1 of those failed servers and still has 1 healthy server remaining, so their requests suffer reduced capacity rather than a total outage. Only a customer assigned the exact same pair would lose service completely, and none exists.

blocks.task: Switch to shuffle shards and send one customer's poison request

blocks.text: The numbers grow quickly. With *n* servers and *k* per customer there are *n* choose *k* different shards, the number of ways to pick *k* of *n*: *n* × (*n* − 1) × … for *k* factors, divided by *k* × (*k* − 1) × … × 1, which for eight and two is the 8 × 7 ÷ 2 above. The chance that a second customer has exactly the same ones as a poisoned customer is one in that number. A hundred servers and five per customer give about 75 million shards. Colm MacCárthaigh's team used the idea in Amazon's Route 53 DNS service, where each customer's domain is served by four name servers picked from a pool of 2,048, which gives about 730 billion combinations.[^route53] Shuffle sharding needs one more thing to work: the client must retry on its other servers, so the slowdown from losing one stays a slowdown.

parts.title: Working without the thing that broke

blocks.text: Most large systems divide into two parts. The **data plane** handles customer traffic by serving requests, storing and returning objects, and forwarding packets. The **control plane** manages the data plane by launching servers, pushing configuration updates, and migrating customers between cells. The data plane runs continuously and has a simple design. The control plane runs less frequently, coordinates complex state changes, and fails more often.

A data plane is **statically stable** if it keeps operating unchanged while its control plane is down, running on the last configuration it received without fetching anything new. Engineers often break this property inadvertently. If a server queries a configuration service on every request, or if a local cache expires and must refill from the control plane every few minutes, a control-plane outage will take down the data plane too.

blocks.caption: Two servers and a control plane, in slow motion. In one design the servers ask the control plane on each request; in the other they keep using the configuration they were last sent.
blocks.task: Choose servers that use their last configuration, then fail the control plane

blocks.text: Amazon's architectural guidelines apply the same rule to server capacity. Consider a service spread across three availability zones in a single region (separate groups of datacentres, each with independent power and networking[^zones]) that must survive the loss of one zone. We could plan to launch new servers in the remaining two zones when a zone fails. However, launching servers requires the control plane, and the failure that knocked out the zone might also impair or overload the control plane. A statically stable service pre-provisions enough capacity in every zone. If one zone goes down, the remaining two zones must carry 100% of the traffic, so each zone must hold enough capacity for 50% of the total load. Across all three zones, the fleet runs at 150% of the capacity required for peak traffic. Paying for that extra 50% capacity every day ensures the system does not depend on the control plane during an outage.

On 4 October 2021, at about 15:40 UTC, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp disappeared from the internet for roughly six hours. Santosh Janardhan, Facebook's vice president of infrastructure, published the cause the next day. During routine maintenance, an engineer ran a command to assess the available capacity of the backbone network that connects all of Facebook's datacentres. Instead, the command disconnected every link in the backbone. An automated audit tool was supposed to block such commands, but a bug in the audit tool allowed it to execute.

Facebook's authoritative DNS servers, which translate facebook.com into IP addresses for the rest of the internet, were configured to withdraw their routing announcements via BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) whenever they lost their connection to the datacentres. That rule is sensible when a single location becomes unhealthy. When every datacentre disconnected at once, every DNS server withdrew its routes, making Facebook unreachable across the internet. Losing DNS and backbone connectivity also broke the internal tools engineers needed to diagnose and revert the change. Staff had to travel to the router facilities in person, where the buildings and servers were designed to resist physical entry and unauthorized local changes.

blocks.caption: What needed what on 4 October 2021, simplified from Facebook's account. A part stops when any part it needs stops.

blocks.text: This failure mode is a **dependency loop**, where the tools required to repair system X depend on system X running. S3's status page failed for the same reason on a smaller scale. Engineers introduce these loops easily because each individual dependency makes sense in normal operation: internal tools resolve names using the company's DNS, and remote management traffic runs over the company's backbone network. To spot loops, engineers must maintain an explicit dependency graph like the one in the figure, and maintain an independent recovery path for total outages. That includes out-of-band management access (a separate network with independent links and authentication, reserved for emergencies), an external status page hosted on a different provider, and printed recovery procedures.

Restoring service also required care. As datacentres reconnected, power consumption jumped by tens of megawatts, and caches across the fleet were empty. Engineers restored traffic gradually, following recovery drills they had previously practised.[^power]

Both the S3 and Facebook outages began with an engineer executing a planned change, which is the most common trigger for major incidents. Google's Site Reliability Engineering handbook estimates that roughly 70% of outages result from changes to a live system. Effective defences constrain the change mechanism rather than relying on human perfection, and Amazon's post-mortem for the S3 outage outlines the standard controls.

**Limit what a tool can do in one step.** Amazon modified its capacity tool to remove servers slowly, and to reject any command that would reduce a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. If a tool allows an operator to remove an arbitrary number of servers in one command, someone eventually will. **Make the blast radius small enough to restart.** S3's index subsystem had grown so large that a cold restart took hours; Amazon accelerated an existing plan to partition the index into smaller cells. A cell provides a bounded unit that engineers can restart, test and recover quickly. **Practise recovery.** If no one has executed a full cold restart in years, no one knows how long it will take or where it will stall. **Roll changes out in stages**, one cell or availability zone at a time. Each stage pauses for a set duration and compares the error rate and latency (the signals from Lesson 24) against cells still running the previous version; if metrics degrade, the deployment system halts and rolls back automatically. In Lesson D7 of the design studio, we will design a staged rollout system in detail.

Every one of these controls trades speed and convenience for safety. Staged rollouts make every deployment take longer; out-of-band networks cost money to run and secure; rate limits in administration tools slow down the engineer who genuinely needs to decommission 400 servers at once. When choosing these limits, you must decide what fraction of the system a single mistake is allowed to take down.

blocks.title: Questions to ask of any design
points: What share of customers does one bad server, one bad request, one bad deploy reach?
If the control plane is down for an hour, does the data plane notice?
Do the tools for fixing this system depend on this system?
When did someone last restart it from nothing, and how long did it take?

blocks.caption: Seven questions on blast radius and recovery
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A request that crashes any server it reaches arrives at a service where every customer is spread over all 40 servers, and its client retries. What is the likely result?
choices: The balancer marks the first server unhealthy and stops sending that request type to any server
Retries carry it from server to server, crashing each, until much or all of the fleet is down
The crashed server restarts in seconds, and the retry is answered by a healthy server instead
items.why: Each retry lands on another healthy server and crashes it. Without cells or shuffle shards, one customer's bad input can reach every server.

items.ask: Twelve servers, three per customer, assigned by shuffle sharding. Roughly what are the odds that another customer has exactly the same three servers as a given customer?
choices: 1 in 4
1 in 12
items.why: There are 12 × 11 × 10 ÷ 6 = 220 different sets of 3 servers. Only a customer assigned the exact same set loses all 3 servers when those machines crash.

items.ask: What do cells give up in capacity, compared with one shared fleet of the same size?
choices: Throughput: every request passes through the router, which caps the fleet at what one router can carry
Storage: each cell keeps a full copy of every customer's data, so the fleet needs more disks
Pooling: each cell holds spare capacity for its own peaks, so the fleet as a whole runs emptier
items.why: Independent cells cannot borrow each other's headroom. The router is thin and can be replicated, and each cell holds only its own customers' data.

items.ask: Which design is statically stable when its configuration service goes down?
choices: Servers fetch their configuration on each request and fail fast with a clear error if they cannot
Servers keep serving with the last configuration they received, and pick up changes when it returns
Servers cache their configuration for five minutes, then refetch it before serving more requests
items.why: Static stability means the data plane needs nothing new from the control plane to keep working. Fetching per request, or every few minutes, ties the data plane's fate to the control plane's.

items.ask: A service runs in three zones and must carry its full load if any one zone is lost, without launching anything new. How much capacity must it run in total?
choices: Exactly the load, a third in each zone, with launches planned for the rest
3 times the load, the whole load in each zone
1.5 times the load, half of the load in each zone
items.why: If any two zones must carry everything, each needs half the load, and three halves make 1.5 times the load. Planning to launch servers during the event depends on a control plane that may be failing too.

items.ask: Why could Facebook's engineers not undo the backbone change from their desks on 4 October 2021?
choices: The internal tools and remote access they needed ran over the same network and DNS that were down
The command had also deleted the configuration backups, so there was nothing left on any server to restore from
Policy forbade changing the backbone from outside the datacentres at any time
items.why: It was a dependency loop: the tools for fixing the network needed the network. Engineers had to reach the routers in person.

items.ask: Which of these would have stopped the mistyped S3 command from removing too many servers in the first place?
choices: Require a second engineer to read every command typed during an investigation
Make the tool remove capacity slowly and refuse to go below each subsystem's minimum
Add an alert that pages the team when many servers are removed at once
items.why: Limits in the tool stop the mistake whoever makes it. A second reader can miss the same typo, and an alert only fires after the damage is done.

summary: **Blast radius is the share of a system one failure reaches.** Measure it for every server, request, deployment and administrative command.
**A poison request can crash an entire shared fleet.** Client retries carry the crashing request from server to server.
**Cells contain failures.** Run independent copies of the stack, each serving a subset of customers behind a thin router, at the cost of lower capacity pooling.

**Shuffle sharding assigns each customer a random subset of servers.** With 8 servers and 2 per customer there are 28 combinations, so a customer who shares 1 server with an affected customer still has 1 working server left.
**A statically stable data plane keeps running without its control plane.** Servers continue operating on their last known configuration without fetching new state.
**Pre-provision capacity instead of launching servers during an outage.** A service across 3 availability zones that must survive losing 1 zone must run at 1.5 times its peak load at all times.
**Eliminate dependency loops in recovery tools.** The tools required to fix a system must not depend on that system running; maintain an out-of-band management network.
**Most outages are triggered by planned changes.** Rate-limit administrative tools, roll out changes in stages, keep cells small enough to restart quickly, and practise cold restarts.

poison.title: Queries of death
poison.text: Google's engineers call these queries of death. The standard defences are cells or shuffle shards to contain them, and logging the active request to disk before processing it so a server that crashes and restarts can recognize and reject the repeated query.

route53.title: Shuffle sharding at Route 53
route53.text: Route 53 answers DNS queries for its customers' domains, and DNS services are a frequent target of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. With shuffle sharding, a traffic flood aimed at one domain overloads only that domain's 4 assigned name servers, while almost every other domain shares at most 1 or 2 of those servers. Colm MacCárthaigh described this design in a 2014 talk and later in the Amazon Builders' Library.

zones.title: Availability zones
zones.text: An availability zone consists of one or more datacentres within a region, built with independent power, cooling and networking a few kilometres from other zones so that a fire or power outage in one does not affect the rest. Zones sit close enough together for network round-trip latencies of 1 to 2 ms, yet far enough apart to fail independently.

power.title: Turning a datacentre back on
power.text: When a datacentre jumps from idle to full load, its power draw spikes all at once, which can trip electrical breakers. Its caches also start cold, so every request in the first wave misses the cache and hits the underlying databases (the thundering herd problem from Lesson 15). Facebook ramped traffic back up in stages to prevent both problems.
